item.title: Iran, Venezuela and Canada Are Testing the Limits of US Power
item.description: Other nations are still reluctant to oppose the US, but now they are also reluctant to support it.
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Levin

item.title: Ambani’s Tech Titan IPO Story Isn't Yet Credible
item.description: Having gone from petrochemicals prince to communications czar and media mogul, India’s second-richest tycoon now wants to be a tech titan. Or at least, that’s how Mukesh Ambani is hawking his digital empire — not as a boring wireless company collecting $2.25 a month from an average user, but as a hotbed of globally valuable innovation.
item.dc:creator: Andy Mukherjee

item.title: Hanwha Aerospace Has Work to Do After US Army Win
item.description: South Korea’s largest defense firm scored a surprise win when it landed its first major contract with the US Army. To turn that foothold into a lasting business and avoid a “Buy-American” backlash, Hanwha Aerospace Co. must now beef up local production.
item.dc:creator: Juliana Liu

item.title: The NBA Punishes Clippers Fans for the Team and Kawhi Leonard’s Sins
item.description: On Wednesday, the NBA imposed one of the toughest penalties in its history. Citing deals it says were designed to circumvent the salary cap, the league stripped the Los Angeles Clippers of five first-round draft picks, fined the team $30 million, suspended owner Steve Ballmer and two executives, and ordered player Kawhi Leonard to pay $700,000.
item.dc:creator: Adam Minter

item.title: T-Mobile Merger: Elliott Is Back Yet Again With Hedge Fund Activism 101
item.description: Elliott Investment Management doesn’t need to come up with new ideas to make money. The US hedge fund activist holds so much sway that it can just throw its weight behind a worry already circulating among investors and be the force that makes a company take it seriously. Its latest such opportunity is thwarting an unpopular $255 billion merger between Deutsche Telekom AG and T-Mobile US Inc.
item.dc:creator: Chris Hughes

item.title: The Pushback Against AI Songs Is Music to My Ears
item.description: Good news for fans of music produced by actual musicians: Some important victories are being won in the war against AI slop and trickery.
item.dc:creator: Dave Lee

item.title: US Canada Trade War Betrays Decades of Cooperation
item.description: We picked a helluva time to go RVing in Canada. My wife and I crossed the border in Maine as trade talks in Washington were collapsing, and we awoke to news of a major escalation in tariffs and even talk of war. It made for some awkward moments in the days that followed.
item.dc:creator: Frank Barry

item.title: Fighting Financial Crime and Shell Companies Shouldn’t Be So Hard
item.description: “Follow the money” has long been a useful strategy for federal law enforcement. So why has the Treasury Department gutted an effort to make it easier?
item.dc:creator: The Editors

item.title: New York Can Create a Sovereign Wealth Fund
item.description: In the fall of 1975, New York City stood at the edge of bankruptcy. The federal government’s answer to a call for assistance, memorably, was no. The city’s own answer came in large part from an unlikely place: its municipal unions, whose pension funds put substantial sums behind the effort to keep New York afloat.
item.dc:creator: Nicolas S. Rohatyn

item.title: Chevron Shows Why Venezuela’s Oil Boom Remains a Distant Prospect
item.description: In a momentous week for Venezuela, Chevron Corp. delivered the sequel to the White House’s blockbuster oil deal. Except that it’s more of a prequel. While the US oil major’s new multi-billion dollar investment in Venezuela would appear to confirm that President Donald Trump’s own venture there will soon bring barrels flooding back into the global market, it actually serves to highlight the challenge of turning rhetoric into reality.
item.dc:creator: Liam Denning

item.title: Global Bond Turbulence Reflects Japan’s Orderly Exit From Decades of Anomaly
item.description: A new explanation for the global ruckus in sovereign bonds is becoming popular: Maybe markets and economies are simply returning to normal. After all, weren’t the preceding years marked by an extraordinarily abnormal constellation of economic circumstances, policy responses and borrowing costs? item.dc:creator: Jonathan Levin

item.title: Private Equity Couldn’t Sell Anything. Until Tax Increases Loomed
item.description: Private equity has been living through a nightmare in recent years. Zombie companies are clogging up portfolios because selling them at prices managers wanted has been nigh on impossible. Firms have resorted to ever more convoluted ways to return cash to their investors, including selling assets to themselves and taking on new forms of borrowing.
item.dc:creator: Paul J. Davies

item.title: Boomer Pensioners Beware. Britain Is Finally Getting Serious About Its Finances
item.description: The alarming spike in global bond yields and the brutal impact on the UK’s borrowing costs have sharpened Westminster minds about the unpleasant economic choices ahead. Happily, we appear at last to have a government and opposition offering voters serious competing visions on what those choices should be.
item.dc:creator: Rosa Prince

item.title: China’s Paper-Tiger Alliance Shows Why the US Can’t Isolate Iran
item.description: The conflict between the US and Iran is beginning to flare again and President Donald Trump says he couldn’t care less. He’s confident his new plan for an “Economic D-Day” that brings Iran to heel by collapsing its economy is a winner. Perhaps, but making it so will take a great deal of international cooperation. As Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent put it: “You’re either with us or against us.”
item.dc:creator: Marc Champion

item.title: AI Generated Campaign Ads Are Eroding Trust in US Elections
item.description: AI slop is taking over political communication. What could go wrong?
item.dc:creator: Mary Ellen Klas
